issues.legal_issue: Interim directions in a liquidation proceeding should not dispossess a claimant or recast the claimant’s possession before the claimant’s asserted tenancy rights have been adjudicated when those rights have prima facie support.
material_facts: The claimant asserted a sub-tenancy agreement with the company, and the company’s board had passed a special resolution affirming that agreement.
The landlord’s counsel stated that the landlord had orally consented to the sub-tenancy; this information had not been before the appellate court that imposed the challenged directions.
The claimant was in possession of a major portion of the premises when the liquidator was appointed.
The claimant’s suit to establish her tenancy rights remained pending, and those rights had not been determined.
The challenged directions placed the premises in the liquidator’s possession, recast the claimant as the liquidator’s agent, and required increased monthly compensation and a security deposit.
issues.conclusion: The directions dispossessing the claimant and changing the character of her possession were not warranted at the interlocutory stage. The Court substituted an interim arrangement under which she could remain pending the suit, subject to furnishing security; if she failed to do so, the challenged directions would revive. The merits of the suit remained undecided.
issues.legal_principle: The Bombay Rent Control Act may protect a sub-tenant, and a company’s liquidation and appointment of a liquidator do not by themselves alter the company’s rights in relation to its landlord or tenants. Tenancy rights may not be assets for liquidation purposes. Where the asserted tenancy has prima facie support and remains to be adjudicated, interim arrangements should not determine the claim by dispossession or by changing the claimant’s status; the Court may protect the company’s interests pending adjudication through security. The Court did not decide whether the sub-tenancy was genuine or legally valid.

rule.if: interlocutory_appeal_in_liquidation_proceeding and claimant_in_possession_before_liquidator and tenancy_claim_has_prima_facie_support and tenancy_rights_unadjudicated and liquidator_directed_to_dispossess_or_recast_claimant_possession

predicates.interlocutory_appeal_in_liquidation_proc: The dispute arises in an interlocutory appeal in a proceeding to wind up a company.
predicates.claimant_in_possession_before_liquidator: The claimant was occupying the disputed premises before the liquidator took control of them.
predicates.tenancy_claim_has_prima_facie_support: Evidence such as the company’s formal affirmation of the tenancy and the landlord’s consent supported the claimant’s tenancy claim at a preliminary level.
predicates.tenancy_rights_unadjudicated: The claimant’s suit to establish the tenancy rights remained pending and no final decision had been made on those rights.
predicates.liquidator_directed_to_dispossess_or_rec: An interim order directed the liquidator to take possession or changed the claimant’s occupancy into possession on the liquidator’s behalf.

issues.definition: When a claimant in a company-liquidation dispute was already occupying the premises, has preliminary support for a tenancy claim that remains undecided, and faces an interim direction to be dispossessed or have the character of that possession changed, the dispossession directions are replaced by continued occupation subject to security.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s request for possession of premises held by a liquidator may be refused where the liquidator gives relevant reasons for retaining possession, including the need to store company records and a proposal to revive the company.
material_facts: The landlord sought an order requiring the liquidator to surrender the flat, including symbolic possession of the portion occupied by the claimant asserting a sub-tenancy.
The liquidator stated that the portion in its possession was needed to store the company’s books.
A proposal for revival of the company was under consideration when the appellate court ruled.

The landlord argued that the records could be stored elsewhere and that the revival proposal had failed, but the Court declined to require the liquidator to relocate the records and said it could not determine whether the proposal had come to nothing.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere with the refusal to order surrender because the liquidator’s stated need to store the company’s books and the revival proposal were relevant considerations. The landlord remained free to apply again if circumstances changed.
issues.legal_principle: A court need not compel a liquidator to store company records elsewhere when the liquidator’s stated need to retain the premises is a relevant consideration. A proposal to revive the company may also be relevant to whether the liquidator should retain possession. The Court found the reasoning consistent with the approach in Ravindra Ishwardas Sethna and Anr. v. Official Liquidator, High Court, Bombay and Anr., while noting that the lower court had considered that decision inapplicable to the facts before it.

predicates.landlord_appeal_in_liquidation_proceedin: A landlord appeals in a company-liquidation proceeding against refusal to order surrender of premises.
predicates.landlord_seeks_surrender_of_premises: The landlord asks the court to require the liquidator to give up premises held for the company.
predicates.liquidator_needs_premises_for_company_re: The liquidator states that the premises are needed to store the company’s records or books.
predicates.company_revival_proposal_under_considera: A proposal to revive the company is under consideration when the court decides whether the liquidator should retain the premises.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks surrender of premises held in a liquidation proceeding and the liquidator needs them for company records while a revival proposal is under consideration, the refusal to order surrender is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A special leave petition challenging a single judge’s order becomes infructuous when the appeal against that order has already been dismissed and a separate special leave petition challenges the appellate dismissal.
material_facts: A special leave petition challenged a single judge’s order.
While that petition was pending, the appellant’s appeal against the single judge’s order was dismissed by a division bench.
A separate special leave petition challenged the division bench’s dismissal.
issues.conclusion: The special leave petition challenging the single judge’s order had become infructuous and was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Where an appeal against the challenged order has been dismissed and the appellate dismissal is itself challenged in a separate proceeding, the earlier special leave petition challenging the original order is infructuous.

predicates.special_leave_petition_against_single_ju: A special leave petition challenges an order made by a single judge.
predicates.appeal_against_that_order_already_dismis: An appeal against that order has been dismissed before the special leave petition is decided.
predicates.separate_petition_challenges_appellate_d: A separate petition challenges the dismissal of the appeal.

issues.definition: When a petition challenges a single judge’s order, the appeal against that order has already been dismissed, and a separate petition challenges the appellate dismissal, the first petition is infructuous.
